I don't have a hypothesis left that's likely to improve this benchmark. So this iteration tests a general-purpose
feature, checking that it doesn't slow the benchmark down: during the existing copy pass, also check whether the input
is already in ascending order, and if so return without sorting. That helps real callers who often pass
already-sorted arrays. The benchmark's inputs are random, so the best outcome here is "no slowdown".
The change tracked, during the copy loop, whether the input was already in ascending order, and skipped the sort if it
was. It made the benchmark's random inputs clearly slower: 0.444 ms against about 0.29 ms. With so few calls, the
copy loop runs before the JIT has fully optimized it, so even one extra comparison per element costs about 50%. An
already-sorted shortcut would need its own separate check that exits at the first out-of-order pair.

#18 showed the copy loop is sensitive because it runs before the JIT has optimized it, so per-iteration overhead

The change unrolled the write-back loop to copy four elements per iteration. It scored 0.291 ms, the same as the
unchanged code's 0.288 ms, so the write-back loop isn't a bottleneck.

The #18 note suggested a cheaper way to detect already-sorted input: a separate pass before the copy that stops at the
first out-of-order pair. On random input that stops after a couple of elements, so it should cost almost nothing.
This run checks that it doesn't slow the benchmark down. It's a general feature for callers who pass sorted arrays,
and I can only keep it if the benchmark doesn't get slower.
